4. The facts of the case relevant for disposal of the Rule, in brief, are that the petitioners in all the four writ petitions are lessees of property of Ain Uddin Haider and Faizunnessa Waqf Estate for 99 years. Their claim is that they have been in lawful possession of the  property) since the  grant of their respective leases and that during the latest land survey the property in question was recorded in the name of the Waqf Estate. It is further stated in the petition that a Title Suit being No. 809 of 2008 was filed for declaration of title, which is pending in the Court of Additional District Judge, Dhaka. It is admitted in the petition that' after the eviction notice dated 7-2-2008 the structures and buildings standing on the petitioner's land were demolished during the eviction drive on 13-2-2008, which was reported in the Daily Samokal on 15-2-2008 (Annexure-P). 

 5. During the course of hearing the petitioners filed several affidavits with the view to amending the petition. Essentially the gist of the amendments is that while LA Case No. 90/1965-66 was pending, LA Case No. 5/1972-73 'was started· for the 'purpose of acquiring land in order to establish the head- quarters for the Rakkhi Bahini. By the two petitions for amendment, the petitioners drew our attention to the fact that two LA cases were proceeding at the same time in respect of the same property and also that the Rakkhi Bahini for whom the land vas proposed to be acquired in LA Case No. 5/1972-73 was abolished in 1975 and, therefore, the purpose of the LA Case was no longer in existence, and the continuation of this LA case and the acquisition of land thereunder was illegal. 

 6. The Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka (respondent No.6) filed affidavit-in-opposition stating the position of the government with regard to the property in question. It is stated in the affidavit in opposition that the land in question was acquired under LA Case No. 5/1 972-73 for the purpose of a Government project of the Housing and Settlement Department. All the legal formalities were observed and all the individual owners were paid compensation for the said land and structures in accordance with law and the land of the project finally vested in the government free from all encumbrances. It is further stated that initially 910 acres of land was sought to be acquired in LA Case No. 90/1965-66 for providing land to Ms Eastern Housing Limited and notices under section 3,5(1) and 5(3) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (the 1948 Act) were duly served on 31-5-1966 and 18-7-1966 observing all legal formalities and the possession of the land was handed ever to the requiring body on 19-4-1966 (sic) including the disputed land of the writ petition. It is stated that a total area of 662.0951 acres of land was finally acquired and published in the gazette notification under section 5(7) of said Act and a deed of transfer was made in favour of the requiring body on 17-6-1971. It is admitted that a number of writ petitions were filed challenging the fact that Ms Eastern Housing Limited was a private organisation and considering such matter' the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka passed an order of derequisition in favour of the petitioners of those cases. Thereafter, on the proposal of the Government Housing and Settlement Department an area of 1076 acres of land, including the land which had been acquired in LA Case No. 90/65-66, and some other land was acquired in LA Case No. 5/72-73 for the said Department, upon fulfilling all requirements under the 1948 Act and the said land was handed over to the requiring body on various dates. Out of the total land acquired, 39.89 acres of land was derequisitioned and a total of 1036.11 acres of land, including the disputed land of the petitioners, was finally acquired and published in the gazette notification under section 5(7) on 15-10-1974, 21-8-1989 and 20-9-1990 respectively. Thus, the land vested in the government free from all encumbrances. It is further stated in the affidavit in opposition that Writ Petition No. 2750 was previously filed challenging the gazette notification dated 15-10-1974 issued as a result of the second LA Case but in that writ petition the Rule was discharged with specific finding that the land was validly acquired and the petitioners were not entitled to get back the land only on the ground that it was previously acquired in LA Case No. 90/65-66 and derequisitioned. It is further stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the legality and propriety of LA Case No. 5/72-73 was challenged in a number of other writ petitions wherein Rules have been discharged with observation that the requirements of sections 3, 4 and 5 of the 1948 Act were duly complied with. 

 7. Affidavit-in-opposition and several supplementary affidavits have been filed on behalf of respondent No. 5, namely the Chairman, Jatiya Housing Authority (previously the Department of Housing and Settlement), also affidavits-in-opposition were submitted by respondent No.7, Executive Engineer of Housing and Settlement Division. The gist of the statements made by the respondent Nos. 5 and 7 is that the land in question was validly acquired for the then Housing and Settlement Department in LA Case No. 5/72-73 upon observing all the legal requirements of the 1948 Act. It is further stated that the validity of the notices were previously challenged in a number of writ petitions, which have in due course been discharged by the High Court Division and the decisions have been upheld by the Appellate Division. It is further stated that regarding the selfsame notices, cases in the civil Court are pending. In particular, reference has been made to Title Suit No. 809 of 2008 in the supplementary affidavit of respondent No. 5 dated 8-4- 2008. It is specifically stated that the plaint of the said title suit has been rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the Joint District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka by the order dated 23-3-2008, holding that there is a bar to any suit challenging the requisition notice under section 14(A) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 148. 

 8. The Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, as respondent No. 7 in the other three writ petitions, has made statements similar to those made by him in Writ Petition No. 1539 of 2008, as stated earlier. 

 9. Mr Md Asadullah, learned Advocate appearing along with Mr Md Helal Uddin Mollah, learned Advocate for the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 1539 of 2008, submits that the land in question was initially acquired for Eastern Housing Limited, a private company and, therefore, does not satisfy the requirement that it should be acquired for a public purpose. He further mentions that since civil suits concerning the same property are pending before the competent civil Court, the issuance of the impugned notice for eviction is unlawful. In this regard, he refers to Syed Mohammad Salem Azam vs Bangladesh 47 DLR (AD) 38. The learned Advocate points out that while LA Case No. 90/65-66 was being processed, there were numerous writ petitions filed before the Hon'ble High Court Division challenging the acquisition and subsequently the said writ petitions were withdrawn on the information supplied by the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing in those writ cases, to the effect that the land acquired in LA Case No. 90/65-66 had been ordered to be derequisitioned and accordingly, the Rules were discharged. as being infructuous. He submits that the order of derequisitioning the land in December, 1973 clearly shows that LA Case No. 90/65-66 was still pending when LA Case No. 5/72-73 was commenced for the same land. He further submits that the acquisition of the property in LA Case No. 5/72-73 was for the purpose of establishing the headquarters of the Jatiya Rakkhi Bahini, which itself was abolished in 1975 and, therefore, the purpose for which the acquisition was proposed was no longer in existence and the land in question must be returned to the petitioners in accordance with the order of derequisition. He further points out that while LA Case No. 90/65-66 was pending in respect of requisition for Ms Eastern Housing Limited, the same land could not be the subject matter of further requisition in LA Case No. 5/72-73 for another purpose, namely the headquarters of the Rakkhi Bahini. He submits that this legal aspect was not agitated in any of the earlier writ petitions or before the Appellate Division. The proceedings of the two LA Cases were being carried on simultaneously in order to circumvent, the earlier order of derequisition, therefore the actions taken under the later LA Case being No. 5/72-73 were illegal, mala fide and malice in law. In this regard, he refers to Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh 33 DLR (AD) 201. 

 10. The learned Advocate for the petitioner next submits that the petitioners land forms part of the Ain Uddin Haider and Faizunnessa Waqf Estate and it was published in the record of rights on 27-7- 2005. He submits that the Khatian notification dated 31-7-2005 showing Ain Uddin Haider and Faizunnessa Waqf Estate to be the owners of the property carries with it a presumption of correctness of the record under section 144(7) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. He submits that such notification by the Government as published in the record of rights overrides any earlier notification under section 5(7) of the 1'948 Act. He submits that it is a legal presumption that the government must know about its earlier notification and, therefore, the effect of the later notification is to strike out the earlier one. He submits that the order of eviction is an affront to the pending judicial proceeding and it is an attempt to pre-empt the judgment in the title suit pending before the competent Civil Court. 

 11. The learned Advocate also points out that the Ministry of Religious Affairs and the Bangladesh Waqf Estate Administrator's Office, have recognised the petitioners as lessees of the Waqf Estate and have also acknowledged the interest of the Waqf Estate in the property in question and, therefore, the action of the government to attempt to evict the petitioners is mala fide and illegal. 

 12. Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No.5, submits that the selfsame property was the subject matter of previous writ petitions and the matter has been finally decided by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 68 of 2004. it has been held in the writ petitions as well as the civil petition for leave to appeal that the land in question was lawfully acquired after complying with all legal formalities and compensation having been paid to the original owners, the land has vested in the government. He points out that the land in question was initially acquired under LA Case No. 90/65-66 and was derequisitioned by order dated 28-8-1973 and subsequently, acquired under LA Case No. 5/72-73 after the publication of notice and observing other legal formalities. He points out that, concerning the selfsame property, Title Suit No. 809 of 2008 is pending before the Civil  Court. The suit was filed by Abdullah Al Mamun who is the Secretary of the Management Committee of the said Waqf Estate. He submits that while the civil case is pending, the instant writ petition is not maintainable. In support, he refers to Shahjadi Begum Waqf Estate vs Bangladesh 2001 BLD (AD) 59 = 7 BLC (AD) 41. By reference to Brahmanbaria Pourashava vs Bangladesh 1999 BLD(AD) 87=51 DLR (AD) 84, he submits that the acquisition, having taken place legally and validly and having been decided by the Appellate Division, cannot again be questioned. 

 13. Ms Syeda Afsar Jahan, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of respondent No.6, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, submits that the property in question was legally and validly acquired by the Government for the requiring body, namely the Department of Housing and Settlement, which is a government organisation, and possession was handed over to the requiring body. She also refers to the finality of decision of the Appellate Division in Civil Petition to leave to Appeal No. 68 of 2004, on the subject matter of these four writ petitions. She further submits that although a proposal was put forward for acquiring land for the purpose of establishing the headquarters of the Rakkhi Bahini, that proposal did not proceed any further in the former LA Case and that the LA Case No. 5/72-73 was for a completely different purpose, namely for acquiring land foe the Department of Housing and Settlement. She submits, therefore, that the statement that two LA Cases for the same land were simultaneously going on is not correct. 

 16. Essentially, the case of the petitioners revolves round the acquisition of land, which was the subject matter initially of LA Case No. 90/65-66. It transpires that at that time some 81 acres of land of the Waqf Estate as well as other land was acquired for the requiring body, namely Ms Eastern Housing Limited, being a private company. The notices under sections 3, 5(1) and 5(3) were duly issued in respect of 910 acres of land including the 81 acres of land of the Waqf Estate. However, subsequently some land was derequisitioned and, we find from the file of the LA Case No. 90/65-66 that, by order dated 6-12-69, notification was issued under section 5(7) notifying the fact of acquisition of 662.0951 acres out of 910 acres. Some land was excluded due to the Court cases pending and some land was derequisitioned, according to the note sheets of the said LA Case file of the Office of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka. We find from the note sheet dated 7-8-73 of the said file that there was a proposal for requisition and acquisition of some land, which had not yet been handed over to Ms Eastern Housing Limited, for establishment of the Zonal Headquarters of the Rakkhi Bahini but from this tile we do not find any reference to a separate LA Case for the purpose of acquiring land for the Zonal Headquarters of Rakkhi Bahini. It appears that so far as the proposal for land to be acquired for the Rakkhi Bahini is concerned, the land was proposed to be requisitioned out of the land already requisitioned for Ms Eastern Housing Limited. We also find from that file that, by 4 four orders dated 17-8-1973, 24-8-1973, 8-9-1973 and 18-10-1973 64.8781 + 14.70+ 158.4481 + 183,0237=421.0499 acres of land was released from the housing scheme  of Ms Eastern Housing Limited for use of the Rakkhi Bahini. However, it is revealed from the same filed note dated 17-8-1973, 8-9-1973 and 18-10-1973 that there are references to LA Case No. 5/72-73 and to the request for acquisition of land for a housing scheme. 

 18. We may also refer to the noting dated 29-3- 70 of the file of LA Case No. 90/65-66 where the Kanungo is directed to prepare a final award in view of the notification No. DA-3/70/27 dated 19-1-70. Thus, quite clearly the process of requisition and acquisition started in LA Case No. 90/65-66 was concluded by the said notification published on 19- 1-70. Therefore, process of LA Case No. 5/73-73 was commenced. Thus, clearly the two LA Cases were not being processed simultaneously. 

 20. From the annexures to the writ petition, we find the decision of the Appellate Division passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 68 of 2004 (Annexure-F) in which the judgment and order dated 11th August, 2003 passed in Writ Petition No. 2934 of 2001 was challenged has been annexed in the affidavit-in-opposition on behalf of the respondent No.5 dated 6-5-2008. The said Judgment of the High Court Division shows that in that writ petition the subject matter was the gazette notification dated 15-10-74 issued as the result of LA case No. 5/72-73. The petitioners of that writ petition challenged the acquisition of the properties of the Waqf Estate, which had previously been acquired in LA Case No. 90/65-66. From the judgment passed in that writ petition, we find that the government by filing affidavit in opposition gave details of notices issued under sections 3, 5( 1), 5(3) and 5(7) of the 1948 Act and also mentioned about the derequisition of land of that LA Case No. 90/65- 66 and subsequent acquisition of 1076 acres of land in the same Mouza, (including those previously requisitioned) in the later LA Case being No. 5/72- 73 in favour of the Government Housing and Settlement Directorate and notices were duly issued and possession handed over to the requiring body on 23- 11-72, 25-8-73, 28-11-73, 5-8-74, 5-3-77 and on some other subsequent dates. Notification under section 5(7) was finally published on 15-10-74, 21- 8-89 and 4-9-90. It is also apparent from the judgment that reference was made to another Writ Petition No. 2750 of 2000, wherein it was held that "since the land was validly acquired in pursuance of the requisition and the land vested in the Government, petitioners have accrued (sic) no right to get back the same only on the ground that their land in question which was previously acquired in LA Case No. 90 of 65-66 was derequisitioned." 

 23. The decision of the High Court Division was challenged in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 68 of 2004, wherein the judgment and order of the High Court Division was upheld dismissing the Petition for Leave to Appeal, which had been filed by one Abdullah Al Mamun, who we find is the Secretary of the Management Committee of the Waqf Estate. We also note that there were some other writ petitions, namely WP No. 7763 of 2005, 7217 of 2002, 2724 of 1999 and 4247 of 2002, wherein the same acquisition Notification dated 15-10-74 was challenged. These Rules were also discharged by the High Court Division and the Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal were filed before the. Appellate Division in Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos. 1152, 1219 and 1660 of 2007. The leave petitions were rejected by the Appellate Division as barred by limitation and also on merit relying upon the fact that the matter had already been decided by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 68 of 2004 on merit. We note from the materials on record that Writ Petitions Nos. 2415, 3349, 3484, 3353, 3480, 3345, 3347, 3346, and 3478 of 1999 were instituted challenging the legality of LA Case No. 5/72-73 and were all discharged with the observation that all the requirements of sections 3, 4 and 5 of the 1948 Act have been duly complied in acquiring the land in LA Case No. 5/72-73 and finding that, therefore, the acquisition-Notification issued under section 5(7) was not issued without lawful authority. 

 24. We also note that the plaint of title suit filed by the Secretary of the Management Committee of the Waqf Estate being Title Suit No. 809 of 2008, which was filed challenging the notification under section 5(7) of the Act published on 4-9-90 has been rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 25. In this connection we may refer to the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh vs Samondra Narayan Mahajan reported in 2006 BLD (AD) 145 = 11 BLC (AD) 226. wherein it has been held that once compensations have been paid there remains no right in the petitioner to get back the land acquired. We may also refer to Brahmanbaria Pourashava vs Bangladesh 1999 BLD (AD) 87, wherein it was held that property validly acquired and vested in the requiring body cannot be claimed by the original owner even if the property is used for a purpose different from the purpose of the original acquisition. In that decision the concept of public purpose was given a broad meaning on the reasoning that if the purpose serves some public use or interest, as opposed to particular interest of an individual, then the purpose would be termed as public purpose. 

 26. In view of the above discussion, particularly in the light of the decisions of the High Court Division and of the Appellate Division which concerned the very same property and also challenged the very same acquisition in LA Case No. 5/72-73, we are of the view that the acquisition was in accordance with law. The same acquisition matter was challenged by the predecessor in interest of the present petitioners being the Secretary, Management Committee of the Waqf Estate both in the Civil Court as well as before the High Court Division and the Appellate Division. The instant writ petitions are nothing more than yet another attempt to nullify the acquisition under LA Case No. 5/72-73, which has been already found by the Appellate Division to have been lawfully done. Since the acquisition was done lawfully and has already been held by both the Divisions of the Supreme Court to have been done validly and the property was found to have vested in the government without any encumbrance, we do not find any merit in the claims of the petitioners. Accordingly, the Rules in Writ Petitions No. 1539 of 2008 and 1948-50 of 2008 are discharged, without any order as to costs.
